results.restated_discrepancy: MCI against cognitively normal controls from resting electrophysiology, accuracy: P-173 NC vs stable MCI 79% (NC vs progressive MCI 82%) against P-129 90.97%. It must not be reported as the recorded conversion claim (P-173 'AUC 0.81' vs P-129 'Acc 94.76').

conditions_argued.1_question: Holds on the printed figures. Both papers classify clinically diagnosed MCI against cognitively normal older adults from resting-state electrophysiology: MEG in P-173, 19-channel EEG in P-129, one channel under the rule ('EEG/MEG'). P-173's two-class contrasts NC vs sMCI and NC vs pMCI are MCI-against-control contrasts. All 76 patients met MCI criteria when the MEG was recorded ('MEG data for this study was collected from 76 MCI patients and 53 age-matched', p. 3), and the 3-year course only divides them into two subsets. The rule does not treat a subset of the MCI label as a different question: condition 3 lists 'the same population subset' as a matched-figure check, and the explanation list names 'label definition'. Both presuppose that pairs differing in subset reach condition 3. Population class: both papers study older adults with MCI by Petersen-type criteria (P-129: 'Neuropsychiatric interviews based on Peterson’s criteria for MCI', p. 2; P-173: 'MCI due to AD', p. 4). P-129's recruitment from cardiac catheterization units is a cohort difference, which condition 1 allows. P-129 does not describe its MCI as vascular or as belonging to another disease class, so the source gives no ground for a Parkinson's-type exclusion.
conditions_argued.2_metric: Holds. Accuracy with accuracy, both from subject-separated cross-validation. P-173's number is the mean accuracy of ten scikit-learn classifiers on its MEG embeddings. It is still the classification accuracy P-173 reports for its method, and classifier choice is an architecture difference, which the rule allows. The averaging is a candidate explanation (naive Bayes, a decision tree and QDA are among the ten), not a metric mismatch.
conditions_argued.3_matched_figure: Holds. P-129 reports no course-defined MCI subsets and no conversion result. P-173 reports no NC-vs-all-MCI contrast and no per-classifier accuracy in the text ('The mean accuracy across the 10 traditional classifiers for each of the network embedding methods are shown in Fig. 3.', p. 9). Its AUCs are only in supplementary figures that are not available here. No figure under the other's condition exists, so nothing dissolves the gap.
conditions_argued.4_uncertainty: Holds, both ways on NC/sMCI. P-173 NC/sMCI 0.79, Wilson n=101 (53+48): centre (0.79+1.9208/101)/(1+3.8416/101)=0.7794, half-width 1.96*sqrt(0.79*0.21/101+3.8416/(4*101^2))/1.0380=0.0787 -> [0.701, 0.858]. P-129 0.9097 (the +/-0.60 is an SD over 20 seeds, not a sampling interval), Wilson n=61: centre (0.9097+1.9208/61)/(1+3.8416/61)=0.8854, half-width 1.96*sqrt(0.9097*0.0903/61+3.8416/(4*61^2))/1.0630=0.0739 -> [0.812, 0.959]. 0.9097 > 0.858 and 0.79 < 0.812; two-sample z = 0.1197/sqrt(0.9097*0.0903/61+0.79*0.21/101) = 2.19. For NC/pMCI 0.82, Wilson n=81 gives [0.7225, 0.8885]. 0.9097 lies outside that interval (one-way; z = 1.59), which the rule accepts. The result does not depend on which course-defined subset is used: P-129's estimate lies outside the interval of every MCI-against-control contrast P-173 prints.
conditions_argued.5_performance_validity: Holds. P-129's cross-subject nested-CV accuracy 0.9097 and AUC 0.950 are below 0.97. Its 0.979 and 0.987 are intra-subject results on separate 27- and 34-subject datasets, not the compared figure. P-173's accuracies are 0.61-0.82.
conditions_argued.6_record: The recorded claim is a misreading: 94.76% is P-129's specificity, P-129 has no conversion analysis, and P-173's 'AUC 0.81' is not in its main text. Condition 6 then directs the judgment to the printed figures, and on those the papers disagree beyond uncertainty. The disagreement therefore does not exist 'only because' of the misreading. It must be reported as the printed accuracies, never as 'AUC 0.81 vs Acc 94.76' or as a conversion conflict.

figures.P-173: Madrid MEG cohort, 53 NC / 48 sMCI / 28 pMCI; mean accuracy of 10 classifiers, 5-fold CV. NC/sMCI 0.79, Wilson n=101 [0.701, 0.858]. NC/pMCI 0.82, Wilson n=81 [0.7225, 0.8885]. (sMCI/pMCI 0.78, Wilson n=76 [0.675, 0.858], not used.)
figures.P-129: Isfahan public EEG dataset, 32 MCI / 29 HC; subject-wise 6x5 nested CV repeated 20 times. Accuracy 0.9097 +/- 0.0060 (SD over seeds), Wilson n=61 [0.812, 0.959]. AUC 0.950. Specificity 0.9476 (the record's 'Acc').

candidate_explanations: Classifier averaging (P-173): 'To assess performance irrespective of a particular classifier, we averaged the classification accuracy of ten popular classifiers' (p. 7). P-129 reports one tuned transformer.

Label definition and subset (P-173): 'the stable MCI group (sMCI, n = 48) comprising those patients that still fulfilled the diagnosis criteria of MCI at the end of follow-up, and the progressive MCI group (pMCI, n = 28)' (p. 4). P-129's MCI group is not selected by course.

MCI definition and recruitment. P-173 required hippocampal atrophy ('should thus be considered “MCI due to AD” with an intermediate likelihood', p. 4) and 'a modified Hachinski score ≤ 4' (p. 4). P-129 recruited 'subjects admitted to the cardiac catheterization units at Sina and Nour Hospitals in Isfahan, Iran [28]' (p. 2) and defined MCI by MMSE 21-26 and NUCOG.

Unit of analysis (P-129): signals were 'segmented into non-overlapping 2-second epochs, and then analyzed on an epoch-by-epoch basis' (p. 3), giving 14,420 MCI and 16,282 HC epochs. P-173 uses one network embedding per subject.

Features and validation. P-173 embeds alpha-band MEG mutual-information networks with MG2G under 5-fold CV. P-129 feeds raw 19-channel EEG to a spatio-temporal transformer under repeated nested CV ('All metrics were averaged over the 20 nested CVs, reported as mean ± standard deviation.', p. 6).
Age range: 65-80 in P-173 against 'all aged over 55 years' in P-129 (p. 2).
Neither paper shows any of these to be sufficient.
results.fragility: The qualification rests on two readings: that P-173's course-defined subsets are MCI-against-control contrasts, and that its ten-classifier mean counts as its accuracy. If the operator rejects either reading, the pair fails condition 1 (no shared question), not condition 3 or 4. P-129's own Table 1 gives an MCI mean MMSE of 26.9 +/- 0.7 under an MCI range of 21-26, an internal inconsistency that does not affect the compared accuracy.
results.reason: On the printed figures every condition holds. Both papers classify MCI against cognitively normal controls from resting MEG/EEG. P-173's 79% (NC vs stable MCI) and P-129's 90.97% each lie outside the other's Wilson interval (z = 2.19), and neither paper reports the other's condition. The recorded conversion claim is a misreading and must not be reported. The discrepancy to report is the printed accuracy gap, with classifier averaging, the course-defined subsets, recruitment and epoch-level analysis as candidate explanations that neither paper shows to be sufficient.

results.restated_discrepancy: MCI against cognitively normal controls from resting electrophysiology, accuracy: P-173 NC vs stable MCI 79% (NC vs progressive MCI 82%) against P-153 93.96% (Dataset I). It must not be reported as the recorded conversion claim. P-153 and P-129 (C-95) appear to analyse the same Isfahan dataset against the same P-173 figures, so if both pairs are reported they should be reported as one discrepancy with two analyses of that dataset.

conditions_argued.1_question: Holds on the printed figures, for the same reasons as C-95. P-153 discriminates 'MCI from normal subjects' (p. 1) using 'the dataset in Ref. [24] ... recorded in Noor Hospital of Isfahan Province' (p. 3): 61 people over 55, with MCI defined by MMSE 21-26 and NUCOG 75-86.5. Those are the same criteria and the same N as P-129's dataset, with the class counts reversed (29/32 vs 32/29). P-153's own text says nothing about cardiac units. P-173's NC vs sMCI and NC vs pMCI are MCI-against-control contrasts in MCI patients diagnosed at the time of recording, and the course-defined subsets are a label-definition difference, which the rule handles at condition 3 and as a candidate explanation. MEG against 19-channel EEG is one channel.
conditions_argued.2_metric: Holds. Accuracy with accuracy. P-153's figure is the mean over three random subject-level train/test splits, and P-173's is a ten-classifier mean under 5-fold CV. Both are classification accuracy.
conditions_argued.3_matched_figure: Holds. P-153 reports no course-defined subsets and no conversion result. P-173 reports no NC-vs-all-MCI contrast. P-153's Dataset II result (Emotiv, 78.65%) is not P-173's condition: it uses another dataset and another headset, it is not MEG, and it has no course-defined subsets. Its non-tensor 89.54% (Table 2) is P-153's own baseline, also not P-173's condition. No figure under the other's condition exists.
conditions_argued.4_uncertainty: Holds, one way, which the rule accepts ('One study's estimate must lie outside the other's 95% interval'). P-173's intervals are as in C-95: NC/sMCI [0.701, 0.858], NC/pMCI [0.7225, 0.8885]. P-153's 0.9396 lies outside both. P-153 reports no interval. Wilson with n=20 test subjects: centre (0.9396+1.9208/20)/(1+3.8416/20)=0.8688, half-width 1.96*sqrt(0.9396*0.0604/20+3.8416/(4*20^2))/1.1921=0.1190 -> [0.750, 0.988]. That interval contains 0.79 and 0.82, so the exclusion is one-way. Pooling the three splits (n=60) gives [0.849, 0.977], and then the exclusion holds both ways. Two-sample z with n=20: 2.24 against NC/sMCI and 1.75 against NC/pMCI.
conditions_argued.5_performance_validity: Holds. 0.9396 is below 0.97, and so is the best single split (96.52%). Table 5 is internally inconsistent: sensitivity 96.07% and specificity 96.98% with 9 MCI / 11 healthy per test split imply an accuracy near 0.45*96.07+0.55*96.98 = 96.6%, not 93.96%. Either value is below 0.97 and above both of P-173's intervals, so conditions 4 and 5 are unchanged, but the report should say that the figure is inconsistent with its own sensitivity and specificity.
conditions_argued.6_record: The record misreads P-153's task: it is detection of current MCI, not conversion. Condition 6 directs the judgment to the printed figures, and on those the one-way exclusion holds with no matched figure.

figures.P-173: NC/sMCI 0.79, Wilson n=101 [0.701, 0.858]. NC/pMCI 0.82, Wilson n=81 [0.7225, 0.8885]. Mean of 10 classifiers, 5-fold CV.
figures.P-153: Dataset I (Isfahan, 29 MCI / 32 healthy): accuracy 0.9396, mean of three random 41/20 subject splits, no interval. Wilson n=20 [0.750, 0.988]; n=60 [0.849, 0.977]. Best split 0.9652. Table 5 lists sensitivity 0.9607 and specificity 0.9698 for the same row. Dataset II (Emotiv, 40 subjects): 0.7865.

candidate_explanations: Classifier averaging (P-173): 'To assess performance irrespective of a particular classifier, we averaged the classification accuracy of ten popular classifiers' (p. 7).

Selection on the evaluation splits (P-153). Component number: 'the value of the variable related to the number of components (R) in the tensor analysis is selected using the classification accuracy assessment and in accordance with the best accuracy in each of the methods.' (p. 10). The 1.5-minute patch and the 60 micro-bands were also chosen by classification accuracy ('According to the results, the best case was related to the time patch of 1.5 min', p. 10).

Label definition and subset (P-173): 'the stable MCI group (sMCI, n = 48) comprising those patients that still fulfilled the diagnosis criteria of MCI at the end of follow-up, and the progressive MCI group (pMCI, n = 28)' (p. 4).

Dataset and hardware: the same P-153 pipeline gives 'average classification accuracy of 93.96% and 78.65% for the first and second datasets, respectively.' (p. 1), a within-method dataset effect of 15 points.

Unit of analysis (P-153): the test tensor holds 400 patches ('5 × 5 × 60 × 400', Table 6, p. 11), and subject labels come from 'voting on the labels of the timepieces of each test subject' (p. 4). But 93.96% is not a mean of three 20-subject vote accuracies (such means are multiples of 1/60), so the unit behind the reported figure is unclear.

Sample size and validation: '41 subjects (20 MCI and 21 healthy) for training process and 20 subjects (9 MCI and 11 healthy) for test, are randomly selected each time.' (p. 4), against 5-fold CV on 81-101 subjects in P-173.
MCI definition and age: 'MCI due to AD' with hippocampal atrophy, aged 65-80 (P-173), against MMSE 21-26 / NUCOG-defined MCI over 55 (P-153).
Neither paper shows any of these to be sufficient.
results.fragility: This pair depends on the same condition-1 readings as C-95 (course-defined subsets; ten-classifier mean). It also meets condition 4 one way only at the conservative n=20, and P-153's headline accuracy is inconsistent with its own sensitivity and specificity.
results.reason: On the printed figures every condition holds. Both papers classify MCI against cognitively normal controls from resting MEG/EEG. P-153's 93.96% lies outside both of P-173's Wilson intervals (NC/sMCI [0.701, 0.858]; NC/pMCI [0.7225, 0.8885]), which meets the rule's one-way test, neither paper reports the other's condition, and neither figure is near ceiling. The recorded conversion claim is a misreading. The discrepancy to report is the printed accuracy gap, with P-153's selection of its settings on the evaluation splits, its internally inconsistent Table 5 and P-173's classifier averaging as candidate explanations that neither paper shows to be sufficient.

results.restated_discrepancy: None needed. The recorded pair holds: P-186 AUC 0.957 (1-year-ahead, NM+MRI; also 0.912 at 6 months) against P-179 AUC 0.826 for 36-month MCI-to-AD conversion in ADNI-1.

conditions_argued.1_question: Holds. Both papers predict conversion from MCI to AD within 36 months in ADNI-1 MCI patients (P-179: 'If conversion happens within three years, we deﬁne these MCI patients as having progressive MCI (P-MCI)', p. 2; P-186: 'converting to AD any time before the last follow-up time, i.e., 36th month, are called MCI progressors (MCIp)', p. 3). The shared channel is structural MRI. P-179 combines baseline FreeSurfer ROI volumes with blood SNP and mRNA, and 'sMRI imaging made the greatest predictive contribution' (p. 8). P-186 combines MRI morphometry with neuropsychological measures. The multimodal clause therefore applies. Single-visit against longitudinal input is an allowed difference: condition 3 lists 'the same single-timepoint input' as a matched-figure check, so it is not a bar under condition 1.
conditions_argued.2_metric: Holds. ROC-AUC with ROC-AUC, both from internal 5-fold CV.
conditions_argued.3_matched_figure: Holds. The reader's borderline rests here, and the source does not support it. (a) No figure under the other's condition exists. P-186 has no baseline-only arm; its only baseline-only figure belongs to a cited study (Huang et al.). P-179 has no longitudinal arm and no MRI-only arm. (b) P-186's MRI-only arm is not a matched figure. P-179's condition is MRI + SNP + mRNA from one baseline visit. The MRI-only arm is still a three-point trajectory with a forecast value, so it matches P-179 on neither input, nor predictor set, nor subset. (c) Even taken as the matched figure, at the recorded 1-year horizon it does not agree within uncertainty by the rule's own test. The rule counts a one-way exclusion as a difference beyond uncertainty (condition 4), so two figures agree only when each lies inside the other's interval. MRI-only 1-year 0.905, Hanley-McNeil 35/50: Q1=0.905/1.095=0.8265, Q2=2*0.8190/1.905=0.8599, SE=sqrt([0.905*0.095+34*(0.8265-0.8190)+49*(0.8599-0.8190)]/1750)=0.0366 -> [0.833, 0.977]. P-179's 0.826 lies outside, and the lower bound stays 0.8326-0.8340 over the rounding range 0.9045-0.9055. Only the 6-month MRI-only figure (0.88, [0.813, 0.947]) agrees with P-179. At 6 months P-186's reported model (NM+MRI 0.912, [0.854, 0.970]) still excludes P-179 and is excluded by it (0.912 > 0.9055; 0.826 < 0.854). P-186's MRI-only arm narrows the gap, but it does not show the non-shared channel to be sufficient at the recorded horizon.
conditions_argued.4_uncertainty: Holds, both ways. P-179 0.8260 with 48 P-MCI / 77 S-MCI (Table 1: sensitivity 81.25% = 39/48, specificity 77.92% = 60/77, accuracy 79.20% = 99/125). Hanley-McNeil: Q1=0.826/1.174=0.7036, Q2=2*0.6823/1.826=0.7473, SE=sqrt([0.826*0.174+47*(0.7036-0.6823)+76*(0.7473-0.6823)]/3696)=0.0406 -> [0.7465, 0.9055]. P-186 1-year NM+MRI 0.957 (35/50): Q1=0.9175, Q2=0.9360, SE=0.0249 -> [0.908, 1.000]. Each lies outside the other's interval; z = 0.131/sqrt(0.0406^2+0.0249^2) = 2.75. The registry's 0.912 (6-month, 49/70, SE 0.0297 -> [0.854, 0.970]) also excludes both ways (z = 1.71). Swapping the class roles in Hanley-McNeil narrows every interval, so the exclusions only strengthen.
conditions_argued.5_performance_validity: Holds as written. P-186's 0.957 is below 0.97 (internal 5-fold CV, n=85). Its 0.98 is the ground-truth benchmark using the actual third readings, not the method's figure. P-179's 0.826 passes.
conditions_argued.6_record: Holds. 0.957 and 0.826 are printed figures. The record gives 0.957 and the registry 0.912, but that ambiguity does not change the outcome, since both exclude P-179 both ways.

figures.P-179: MCI-CPS, ADNI-1, 125 MCI (48 P-MCI / 77 S-MCI), 5-fold CV: AUC 0.8260, Hanley-McNeil [0.7465, 0.9055]. Accuracy 79.20% (Table 1; the text says 80.00%), Wilson n=125 [0.713, 0.854]. External ADNI-GO/2 (n=98): AUC 0.7809.
figures.P-186: Linear SVM on three-point trajectories (two observed visits plus a forecast value), 5-fold CV, ADNI-1. NM+MRI: 1-year 0.957 [0.908, 1.000] (35/50); 6-month 0.912 [0.854, 0.970] (49/70). MRI only: 1-year 0.905 [0.833, 0.977]; 6-month 0.88 [0.813, 0.947]. Accuracy (Table 6): NM+MRI 81% at 1 year (Wilson n=85 [0.714, 0.879]) and 84.9% at 6 months (n=119 [0.774, 0.902]); MRI only 83.5% and 79.8%.

candidate_explanations: Input representation and timing (P-186): 'Te method proposed in this paper has recorded the highest classiﬁcation AUC of 95.7% predominantly because of involving the forecasted marker value at the time of conversion as a classiﬁcation feature.' (p. 8). The authors assert this; no baseline-only arm tests it.

Non-shared predictors. P-186's neuropsychological measures: its MRI-only arm gives 0.905/0.88 against 0.957/0.912 with NM ('MRI 13 88.71% (4 ×10−6) 88% (1.3 ×10−6) 13 91.4% (8.7 ×10−7) 90.5% (1.02 ×10−6)', Table 5, p. 9). P-179's blood SNP and mRNA.

Subset-size selection on AUC (P-186). The reported AUC is the best of many marker-subset sizes on the same CV: 'Each biomarker subset is modeled and evaluated for its eﬃcacy through our proposed system.' (p. 4); 'the proposed method delivers a maximum AUC of 91.2% (p value 4.7 ×10−6) and 95.7% (p value 4.1 × 10−7) using 19 and 9 bimodal features, respectively.' (p. 8).

Preprocessing outside the folds (P-186): 'We scale all features to have values between 0 and 1 before the train-test split.' (p. 4). Marker ranking by t-tests on baseline readings is not stated to happen inside the folds.

Outcome window against observed readings (P-186). The 1-year design uses 'three consecutive annual readings, resulting in 35 MCIp and 50 MCIs subjects.' (p. 3), and MCIp means conversion any time before month 36, so an early converter's observed readings can fall at or after conversion.

Eligible population and sample: 85 subjects with three complete annual readings (P-186), against 'SNP, gene expression and sMRI data of 125 MCI patients were downloaded from the ADNI-1 study as the training dataset' (P-179, p. 3).
None is shown to be sufficient. P-186's MRI-only arm narrows the 1-year gap to 0.905 vs 0.826, which still fails the rule's agreement test.
results.fragility: P-186's 1-year MRI-only interval excludes 0.826 by only 0.007, but that matters only if the MRI-only arm is accepted as a matched figure, and condition 3's definition does not support that. The headline exclusion (z = 2.75) is robust. The AUC discrepancy has no accuracy counterpart: P-186's accuracies (81% and 84.9% for NM+MRI) agree with P-179's 79.2%. The report should say that the discrepancy is in AUC only and that P-186's AUC is the maximum over marker-subset sizes.
results.reason: The source supports every condition. Both papers predict 36-month MCI-to-AD conversion in ADNI-1 with MRI shared, both report AUC, and P-186's 0.957 [0.908, 1.000] and P-179's 0.826 [0.7465, 0.9055] exclude each other (z = 2.75). Neither paper reports the other's condition. P-186's MRI-only arm, which the reader treated as the near-match, is still longitudinal. It is not under P-179's condition, and at the recorded 1-year horizon it still leaves 0.826 outside its interval [0.833, 0.977]. The pair qualifies. The candidate explanations are the forecast value at conversion, the neuropsychological channel, subset-size selection and preprocessing outside the folds, none shown to be sufficient. The report should add that the two models' accuracies agree.

results.restated_discrepancy: If the operator reports this operator-named pair anyway, the only wording the sources support is an internal single-scan AUC difference of about 0.05 (P-78 0.832 vs P-182 0.777) at the edge of uncertainty. P-78 itself shows on external data that CDR-SB supervision produces a gap of that size. The pair must not be reported as 90.7% vs 75.85%.

conditions_argued.1_question: Holds. Both papers predict progression from MCI to AD from structural MRI in ADNI MCI patients.
conditions_argued.2_metric: Holds for accuracy (the recorded metric) and for AUC; both papers report both.
conditions_argued.3_matched_figure: Fails. P-78 reports P-182's single-scan condition. Each single-scan comparison is either reconciled by P-78's own figures or fails to clear the test beyond reporting precision. (a) Recorded quantity. P-78's single-scan internal accuracy, 0.763 (0.711-0.816), and P-182's 0.7585 (0.713-0.799) each lie inside the other's interval (z = 0.13). The 90.7 vs 75.85 gap comes from P-78's four-scan input, and P-78 shows this ('Compared to STP, DTP, and TTP, the ACC improved by 14.4 %, 7.7 %, and 3.8 %, respectively', p. 9). (b) External single-scan figures, where the reader missed a row of P-78's Table 6. P-78's full model exceeds P-182 both ways on Dataset A, which is baseline scans only (AUC 0.858 vs 0.777, z = 2.01; accuracy 0.827 vs 0.7585). This survives subject-level recomputation (Hanley-McNeil 91/82 [0.802, 0.914]; Wilson n=173 [0.764, 0.876]). But on the same baseline scans, P-78's ablation '(2) Without CDRSB, which used only binary diagnostic labels' (p. 9) gives AUC 0.812 (0.745-0.872) and accuracy 0.763 (0.699-0.832) (Table 6, p. 10). Binary diagnostic labels are the supervision P-182 uses: its model 'trains to differentiate AD versus CN data' (p. 5). The ablated figures agree with P-182 both ways: 0.777 lies in [0.745, 0.872] and 0.812 in [0.723, 0.831]; 0.7585 lies in [0.699, 0.832] and 0.763 in [0.713, 0.799]; AUC z = 0.82. P-78 therefore shows that one named difference, CDR-SB supervision, is sufficient for the external single-scan gap, and under the brief ('If a paper shows it, the pair fails condition 3') that leg fails. (c) The only remaining leg is the internal single-scan AUC: 0.832 (0.783-0.874) against 0.777, derived interval [0.723, 0.831]. On the same single-scan test the accuracy agrees. 0.832 exceeds P-182's derived upper bound by 0.0008, inside the rounding of the two three-decimal values (the bound runs 0.8307-0.8316 as 0.777 runs 0.7765-0.7775). 0.777 lies 0.006 below P-78's reported lower bound. That interval is narrower than 101 subjects allow: its accuracy interval (width 0.105) is about two-thirds of the subject-level Wilson width (0.671-0.835), consistent with resampling the ~304 test images. A subject-level Hanley-McNeil interval for 0.832 in 101 subjects runs from [0.736, 0.929] to [0.754, 0.910] across class splits 30/71 to 70/31, and every such interval contains 0.777. Two-sample z = 0.055/sqrt(0.0232^2+0.0276^2) = 1.52. By the letter, P-78's reported interval does exclude 0.777, and that is the strongest yes argument. It rests on an interval that understates subject-level uncertainty, on a margin below reporting precision on the other side, and on a metric whose companion accuracy from the same test agrees. I do not find that it establishes a difference the papers' own data leave unreconciled.

candidate_explanations: Input representation, shown sufficient for the recorded accuracy gap by P-78: 'Compared to STP, DTP, and TTP, the ACC improved by 14.4 %, 7.7 %, and 3.8 %, respectively' (p. 9).
Supervision (CDR-SB against binary diagnostic labels), shown sufficient for the external single-scan gap by P-78's Table 6: 'removing CDRSB reduced AUC by 4.6 % and accuracy by 6.4 %' (p. 9).

Training population: P-182's model never saw MCI during training ('used a classification framework in which MCI progression is predicted based on a model that trains to differentiate AD versus CN data.', p. 5). P-78 is trained on longitudinal MCI data.
Region: P-182 uses a hippocampal box ('We first defined a 3D bounding box', p. 2); P-78 uses whole-brain sMRI.

Label and horizon: P-182 requires diagnoses 'obtained at least 18 months apart' (p. 2); P-78 predicts status at 36 months, with 'During the selection process for pMCI subjects, a dynamic data augmentation method was used' (p. 3).
Cohort (external leg): ADNI-3 and OASIS-3 with CDR-defined status, against ADNI-2/GO.
results.reason: The pair fails condition 3. P-78's single-scan internal accuracy (76.3%, 71.1-81.6%) matches P-182's 75.85%, so the recorded 90.7-vs-75.85 gap is the four-scan input. The external single-scan gap (AUC 0.858, accuracy 82.7%), which the reader relied on, is closed by P-78's own ablation without CDR-SB supervision (AUC 0.812, accuracy 76.3%, both agreeing with P-182): a paper-shown explanation. The one remaining leg, internal single-scan AUC 0.832 vs 0.777, clears the rule's test only against a bootstrap interval narrower than 101 subjects allow and by 0.0008 on the derived side, while the accuracy from the same test agrees.
